prompt: Customers receive one email notification when a product they signed up for returns to stock.

intent.desiredOutcome: Customers receive one email notification when a product they signed up for returns to stock.
intent.qualityBrief: A good version handles the happy path cleanly: customer signs up, product restocks, email goes out, record marks as notified. Edge cases to consider: duplicate signups for the same product (deduplicate or allow?), product variants with separate inventory, what happens if a product is deleted, and whether to let customers unsubscribe from emails. The admin page should be scannable at a glance — show status clearly so the merchant knows which notifications succeeded.

plan.dataFlow: When a customer visits a sold-out product page they submit their email via the widget, which records a pending signup keyed to that product variant; a matching widget GET lets the widget render the correct initial state on page load without a form submission. When an inventory replenishment event fires for a variant, the system fetches all pending signups for that variant and, for each, sends a restock notification email and records the outcome — marking the signup as notified on success or as failed with a reason on failure. Signups that have already been notified are skipped so a second restock event never fires a duplicate email. The merchant views every signup and its notification outcome from the admin panel, filtered by status so successes and failures are immediately scannable.

triggers.idempotency: if all pending signups for the variant have already been notified, treat the event as a no-op and make no external calls

Mark a customer's signup as unsubscribed so no future notification is sent for that variant.
Retrieve the product title and variant details from the external platform so the notification email can include meaningful product information.
Retrieve all signups in the pending state for a given product variant so the restock handler knows which customers to notify.
Deliver a one-time back-in-stock email to a customer containing the product name and a link to purchase.
Persist the result of a notification delivery attempt and advance the signup to its terminal state so the audit log is complete and the customer is never emailed again for this signup.
Return a paginated, status-filtered list of signups with their notification outcomes for the merchant admin dashboard.

externalContracts.purpose: Return whether the current customer is already signed up for back-in-stock notification for a given product variant so the widget can render the correct initial state; customer identity is resolved server-side from the Shopify storefront customer access token supplied in the request header, not from a caller-supplied email field.
Register a customer's email address to receive a one-time notification when a specific product variant is back in stock.
Unsubscribe a customer from a back-in-stock notification for a specific product variant.
Return a paginated, filterable list of all back-in-stock signups and their notification outcomes for the merchant dashboard.

edgeCases: A customer submits the widget form twice for the same product variant — the second request must be a no-op that returns success without creating a duplicate signup record.

A duplicate inventory replenishment event is delivered for the same variant after notifications have already been sent — the handler must detect that no pending signups remain and exit before making any email or external API calls.

The email provider rejects delivery for a customer address with a permanent failure (bounce or invalid address) — the attempt must be logged as failed with the rejection reason, the signup marked accordingly, and no retry attempted automatically so the customer is not spammed.
A customer unsubscribes between signing up and the restock event firing — the handler must check signup status before sending and skip any signup not in the pending state.

The product variant is deleted or made unavailable before the restock notification is dispatched — fetching variant details will fail, the affected signups must be marked as cancelled with the reason recorded, and no email is sent.

A restock event carries an inventory quantity that is above zero but the product is still marked as unavailable for purchase — treat the event as a no-op and do not notify customers, preserving the notification for a genuine purchasable restock.

A restock webhook fires a second time for the same variant while notifications for that variant are still in flight — a per-variant advisory lock or atomic status transition from pending to processing must be acquired before fetching pending signups so that the concurrent second delivery finds no pending rows and exits without sending duplicate emails.

The email provider returns a transient failure (timeout or 5xx) rather than a permanent rejection — the attempt is retried up to a fixed maximum number of attempts before being recorded as a terminal failure with a distinct transient-failure reason code, ensuring retryable notifications are not permanently discarded on the first provider hiccup.

hld_v_findings.issue: The external-event trigger has no edge case covering duplicate webhook delivery before any signups have been notified — the idempotency text on the trigger itself addresses the 'all already notified' case, but there is no edgeCase entry handling a scenario where the same restock webhook fires twice concurrently while notifications are still in flight. If two webhook deliveries race, `identify-pending-signups` will return the same pending rows for both, and `send-restock-notification` will fire twice for every customer. The edgeCases list covers only the post-hoc duplicate (edge case 2), not the concurrent in-flight race.
hld_v_findings.fix: Add an edge case that explicitly states how concurrent duplicate webhook deliveries are handled while notifications are in flight — e.g. 'a per-variant advisory lock or atomic status-flip (pending → processing) is acquired before fetching pending signups so that a second concurrent delivery finds no pending rows and exits cleanly.'

hld_v_findings.issue: cancel-signup has usesWorkflow=true, but register-signup — the capability that creates the initial pending row — has usesWorkflow=false. The HLD spec correctly sets usesWorkflow=false on initial-state inserts, but cancel-signup is a single terminal-state writer for the 'unsubscribed' branch, while record-notification-outcome (usesWorkflow=true) is the writer for the 'notified' and 'failed' terminal states. These two write capabilities are triggered by completely different actors (customer-initiated vs. system-automated) and write to the same status column on product_signups, which is correct decomposition — but cancel-signup lists only 'customer email' and 'variant external id' as dataNeeds, with no signup id. Without the row identifier in dataNeeds, the LLD has no anchor to locate and lock the specific row being transitioned, creating a gap where a concurrent notify could race against an unsubscribe on the same record.
hld_v_findings.fix: Add 'signup id' (or equivalent row identifier) to the dataNeeds of cancel-signup so the LLD can perform a targeted, lockable row update rather than a lookup-by-composite-key write.

hld_v_findings.issue: The widget GET requestShape includes 'customer_email' as a caller-supplied field. On a storefront widget, the page context does not reliably expose the customer's email address — it must be discovered from the session/cookie or typed by the user, neither of which the widget can supply as a pre-known value on page load. Requiring email in the GET request means the widget cannot render the correct initial state without prior user input, which defeats the purpose of the endpoint (rendering before form submission).
hld_v_findings.fix: Remove 'customer_email' from the GET requestShape and resolve the customer identity server-side from the session token or Shopify customer context; if email must remain caller-supplied, document an explicit mechanism (e.g. Shopify storefront customer access token) in the contract's purpose so the LLD knows the source.

hld_v_findings.issue: There is no edge case describing what happens when the email provider is temporarily unavailable (timeout, 5xx, network error) as distinct from a hard rejection (bounce, invalid address). Edge case 3 covers hard rejection with no retry, but a transient provider failure has a completely different handling requirement — it may warrant a retry or at minimum a different failure_reason category. Without this distinction the LLD will conflate transient and permanent failures, potentially discarding retryable notifications as permanently failed.
hld_v_findings.fix: Add an edge case that distinguishes transient email provider failures (timeout/5xx) from permanent rejections, and states explicitly whether transient failures are retried (and how many times) or also recorded as terminal failures with a distinct reason code.

hld_v_findings.issue: The product_signups table has no column for storing the failure_reason when a signup is marked failed, yet record-notification-outcome writes a 'failure reason' and the notification_attempts table stores it there. If the admin list-signups capability surfaces failure reason inline (which a 'scannable at a glance' dashboard implies), every display of that reason requires a join to notification_attempts. This is not fatal but the dataFlow description says the merchant views 'notification outcomes' from the admin panel — the LLD will need to decide whether to join or denormalise with no guidance from the plan.
hld_v_findings.fix: Either add a 'failure_reason' column (nullable text) to product_signups for fast inline display, or add an explicit note in the product_signups purpose or queryPatterns that failure reason is always retrieved via join to notification_attempts so the LLD generates the correct query.

platformGaps.gap: No batch email mutation exists for multiple recipients in a single Shopify or platform call, so per-signup email delivery inside the for_each loop requires one platform.email.send call per customer.
platformGaps.mitigation: Each signup iteration calls platform.email.send individually inside a try_catch; continueOnError=true on the for_each ensures a single send failure does not abort the remaining recipients.
platformGaps.uxImplication: Partial-success outcomes (some customers notified, some failed) are possible; the admin dashboard must display per-signup status so the merchant can identify and manually address failed deliveries.

platformGaps.gap: The inventory_levels/update webhook fires for every inventory adjustment (including decrements and transfers), not exclusively for zero-to-positive transitions.
platformGaps.mitigation: The recipe checks payload.available > 0 in a decision step and exits early when the quantity is not positive, ensuring decrements and same-level adjustments are treated as no-ops.

platformGaps.gap: Shopify does not provide a storefront customer access token in webhook payloads, so the widget GET route cannot rely on a Shopify-issued identity token; it falls back to a caller-supplied customer_email query parameter.
platformGaps.mitigation: The widget GET and POST routes accept customer_email directly in the request; the app trusts the value as supplied by the widget which reads it from the logged-in customer context via host.context.
platformGaps.uxImplication: Widget must pre-fill customer_email from the logged-in customer context before making API calls; for guests the email field must be shown as a manual input.

emailSpec.purpose: Notify a customer that a product variant they signed up for is back in stock and prompt them to purchase before it sells out again.

starterContent.subject: {{productTitle}} is back in stock!
starterContent.body:
Great news! {{productTitle}} — {{variantTitle}} is back in stock and available to purchase now.

Shop now before it sells out →

You're receiving this email because you signed up for a back-in-stock alert. You will not receive further notifications for this item.

uxExpectations.storefront: Widget should appear on sold-out product pages as a compact inline form — one email input field and a single 'Notify me' button. For logged-in customers, pre-fill the email field from host.context and allow one-click submission. Once signed up, replace the form with a confirmation message and an 'Unsubscribe' link. After the variant is restocked, the widget should revert to the standard add-to-cart UI.
uxExpectations.admin: Dashboard should lead with a status-tab navigation (All / Pending / Notified / Failed / Unsubscribed) so the merchant can immediately scan delivery health. Each row should show the customer email, product variant, signup date, and resolution date. Failed rows should surface the failure_reason inline so the merchant can act without drilling into a detail view. A summary count at the top of each tab gives at-a-glance volume.

edgeCases: A restock webhook fires while a previous delivery wave for the same variant is still in progress — the sql_claim atomic UPDATE WHERE status='pending' ensures each signup is claimed by exactly one wave; the second concurrent webhook finds no unclaimed rows and exits cleanly.

A customer holds a terminal signup row (notified, failed, or unsubscribed) and attempts to sign up again for the same variant — the ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING insert returns zero rows and the response returns success=true; the merchant should consider a UI flow to allow re-subscription after deletion of the terminal row if desired.

The notification_attempts table accumulates a failed_permanent row while the product_signups row is simultaneously updated to failed — both writes happen inside the same try_catch catch arm per iteration, but they are not wrapped in a sql_transaction; a crash between the two writes would leave the signup row in notified state with no attempt log, which the sweep cron would later correct.

product_signups.failure_reason is stored inline on the signup row and also in notification_attempts.failure_reason — these two values are written from the same emailError.message source in the same catch arm, so they will always agree; the denormalisation is intentional for fast admin display without a JOIN.

A customer uses two different email addresses to sign up for the same variant — each address creates a distinct signup row (the unique constraint is on customer_email + variant_external_id), and both receive independent notification emails on restock.

The SHOP_DOMAIN environment variable used to construct the product URL is missing at runtime — the compute step would produce a malformed URL; this must be validated at app startup and surfaced as a configuration error rather than silently emitting broken links in notification emails.
